title: Warehouses and dimensional models: OLAP and star schemas
goal: By the end, you can explain why a warehouse keeps payments as one long table of events with small tables of descriptions around it, choose between a star, a snowflake and one big table, keep a shop's history when the shop changes, and say how big warehouses join those tables without moving the long one.
opening:
Picture a small company that runs the program behind card readers in cafés and shops. Each tap of a card is one payment, and each week its finance team asks questions of them all.

On 3 November, the report for 1 to 3 November says the high-risk shops took 21.9 million. The next day, the company moves 50 shops into its high-risk group. A week later, someone reruns the report for the same three days. Now it says 43.1 million, and nobody added a payment.

It's easy to blame the report. The cause is a table with one line per shop, and those lines now say high-risk. It feels natural, since that's how the payments program keeps shops.

Spark 4 for JVM engineers was about the engine, Spark, a program that spreads work over many computers. In this lesson, we'll turn to the tables it reads. We'll shape them for questions about history, decide what the past should say when a shop changes, and see how big engines join them. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: On 4 November, the company moves shop 1 from its low-risk group to its high-risk group. In the reporting copy of the data, it changes the tier on shop 1's one row. On 10 November, finance reruns the report "money taken by risk group, 1 to 3 November". Where does shop 1's money from those three days show up?
options: Under low risk, the group shop 1 was in on those days
Under high risk, the group the row says today
Split between low and high, by date
Nowhere, because changing the row cuts the old payments off from it
warmup.why: The report matches each payment to its shop's row, and there's only one row, which now says high. Overwriting the row rewrote history: the same report over the same days gives a different answer after the change. In this lesson's demo, the high tier's money for those days grows by 97%. Low risk is the answer most people expect, and you only get it if the warehouse kept the old version of the shop as a row of its own. That's the type 2 change of the third section.

sections.h: Reshaping payments for questions: one fact table and its dimensions
sections.body:
Let's start with a question finance asks: how much money did each kind of shop take, on weekdays and at weekends? The payments program keeps its data in a database, a program that stores tables (grids of rows and columns, like a spreadsheet) and answers questions about them.

Three tables matter here. `raw_payments` has one row per payment: its number, the shop, the card's country, the currency, the amount in cents, a status and the time. A status of `CAPTURED` means the money has really moved. `raw_merchants` has one row per shop (the code calls a shop a merchant): its name, a category code, its risk tier and its country. And `raw_mcc` turns each category code into a name such as Travel or Groceries.

Two of those columns need a word. Card companies give every kind of shop a number, a merchant category code (`mcc`); in this track the codes are made up, from 5000 to 5019. And the company sorts its shops into three risk tiers, LOW, MEDIUM and HIGH, by how often their payments go wrong through fraud or customers asking for their money back.

Each fact is written in one place. A shop's category sits on the shop's row, not on each of its payments, so changing it touches one row. That suits the payments program, which finds a few rows by their key, thousands of times a second. Work like that is called operational, or OLTP (online transaction processing). Finance's question is the other kind, analytical work or OLAP (online analytical processing): it reads millions of rows to answer a few questions a day.

Version 1: ask the question of those three tables, in the database that takes the payments. Questions to a database are written in SQL, the language most of them understand, and a question written in it is called a query. This one joins each payment to its shop's row and each shop to its category name. A join matches the rows of two tables on a shared value, the way you'd look up each receipt's shop in a list of shops. Then it keeps the captured payments, groups them by category and kind of day, and adds up each group.

It works once, and then it breaks three ways. The payments database keeps each row's columns side by side, so it reads all seven columns of every payment to use three of them. Column stores and compression, in the Storage track, measured that cost. The big read competes with card readers for the same disks and memory, so checkouts slow down while finance waits. And every analyst writes the date logic again in every question (is this a weekend? which quarter?), a little differently each time.

Version 2: copy the data into a separate database built for such questions, a **data warehouse**, and reshape it on the way. Picture a bookkeeper's journal with card files beside it. The journal has one line per sale: a date, an account number, an amount and nothing else. The card files hold one card per account and one per day, with everything worth knowing about each. To answer a question, you read the journal once and look at each line's cards.

Ralph Kimball, who wrote the standard books on warehouses in the 1990s, gave this shape its names. The journal is the **fact table**, with one row per event. The first thing you decide about it is its **grain**, what one row means: here, one payment. A fact row holds measures, the numbers you add up (`amount_cents`), and keys, numbers that point at rows of other tables.

The card files are **dimension tables**. They describe who, what, where and when, in as many columns as analysts want. `dim_merchant` holds each shop's name, its category already looked up, its risk tier and its country. `dim_date` holds one row per day, with its weekday, a weekend flag, the month and the quarter, so nobody works out a weekend by hand again. Small details with no table of their own, such as the status, stay on the fact row; Kimball calls them degenerate dimensions. Draw the facts in the middle with a line to each dimension, and you get a star. So the design is called a **star schema** (a schema is a set of tables and their columns).

The shape follows from the work. Facts are many and narrow: millions or billions of rows of keys and numbers, written once and never changed. Dimensions are few and wide: hundreds or thousands of rows of text. A question filters and groups by dimension columns and adds up fact columns. In the Try it, a week of payments, one million of them, becomes a fact table of 1,000,000 rows and 7 columns. Next to it sit a 7-row date dimension and a 500-row merchant dimension. Finance's question becomes two joins, a filter and a sum per group.

Each of those joins happens while the question runs. Next, we'll see what changes if we do them once, ahead of time.

try.title: Turn a million payments into a star
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `StarDemo` with the command below. It uses DuckDB, a free analytics database that runs inside your own program, here with every table held in memory. It creates the payments program's three tables, builds the star from them, prints the size of each table and one payment with the dimension rows it points at, then asks finance's question of both shapes.
Before you read the output: how many rows will `dim_date` have, and how many will `fact_payment` have?
Compare the two questions in the source, `operational` and `star`. Which one would an analyst get wrong more easily, and where?

code.title: StarDemo.kt (the tables are built in DemoStar.kt)
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l10.demo

/**
 * A million payments in their operational shape, then the same data as a star: one fact table of
 * events and two dimension tables. Prints the shape of each table, one fact row with the dimension
 * rows it points at, and the analyst's question asked of both.
 */
fun main() {
    duck().use { c ->
        rawTables(c, 1_000_000)
        buildStar(c)
        println("%-14s %10s %8s".format("table", "rows", "columns"))
        for (t in listOf("raw_payments", "raw_merchants", "raw_mcc", "fact_payment", "dim_date", "dim_merchant")) {
            val rows = c.rows("SELECT count(*) FROM $t").first()[0]
            val cols = c.rows("SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = '$t'").first()[0]
            println("%-14s %,10d %8s".format(t, rows, cols))
        }

        val f = c.rows("SELECT * FROM fact_payment WHERE payment_id = 3").first()
        println("one fact row:        payment_id=${f[0]} date_key=${f[1]} merchant_key=${f[2]} card_country=${f[3]} currency=${f[4]} status=${f[5]} amount_cents=${f[6]}")
        val d = c.rows("SELECT day, day_name, is_weekend, quarter FROM dim_date WHERE date_key = ${f[1]}").first()
        println("  its dim_date row:  day=${d[0]} day_name=${d[1]} is_weekend=${d[2]} quarter=${d[3]}")
        val m = c.rows("SELECT merchant_id, merchant_name, category, risk_tier, country FROM dim_merchant WHERE merchant_key = ${f[2]}").first()
        println("  its dim_merchant:  merchant_id=${m[0]} name='${m[1]}' category=${m[2]} risk_tier=${m[3]} country=${m[4]}")

        // the analyst's question: captured volume per category, weekdays against weekends
        val operational = """
            SELECT c.category, dayofweek(p.created_at) IN (0, 6) AS weekend, count(*), sum(p.amount_cents)
            FROM raw_payments p
            JOIN raw_merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id
            JOIN raw_mcc c ON c.mcc = m.mcc
            WHERE p.status = 'CAPTURED'
            GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2"""
        val star = """
            SELECT m.category, d.is_weekend, count(*), sum(f.amount_cents)
            FROM fact_payment f
            JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
            JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key
            WHERE f.status = 'CAPTURED'
            GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2"""
        val (a, ta) = best { c.rows(operational) }
        val (b, tb) = best { c.rows(star) }
        println("captured volume by category and day type (star schema, best of 5: %.0f ms):".format(tb))
        for (r in b) println("  %-12s weekend=%-5s %,8d payments %,18d cents".format(r[0], r[1], r[2], r[3]))
        println("the operational tables give the same answer: ${a == b} (best of 5: %.0f ms)".format(ta))
    }
}

The fact table has as many rows as there were payments, and stays narrow: two keys, a few small details (card country, currency, status) and one measure. The dimensions are tiny. Payment 3 shows how to read a fact row. Its `date_key`, 20261104, leads to a Wednesday in quarter 4, and its `merchant_key`, 483, leads to shop 482, a low-risk grocery shop in France. sections.h: Star, snowflake or one big table: deciding when the joins happen
sections.body:
A star keeps each dimension flat. `dim_merchant` carries the category name itself, copied onto every shop in that category, so anything about a shop is one join away from its payments. The lookup from code to name ran once, when the dimension was built. There are two other ways to store the same descriptions, and what really differs between the three is when the joins happen.

A **snowflake schema** splits the dimensions further. `dim_merchant` keeps only the category code, a `dim_category` table names it, and a `dim_category_group` might sit above that. Drawn out, the star grows branches, hence the name. (It's older than Snowflake, a warehouse that companies rent as a cloud service, and has nothing to do with it.) Each description is now stored exactly once, the rule called normalization in Designing a schema: normalization and constraints, in the SQL track. The cost is one more join per level in every question, to save a few kilobytes in tables of a few thousand rows. Analysts mostly prefer the star, and so would I.

**One big table** (OBT) goes the other way. It copies every dimension column onto every fact row, so the joins happen once, when the table is written, and every question reads one table. In a database that keeps a row's columns side by side, that would be wasteful: the shop's name repeated on every one of its payments. A column store keeps each column apart and squeezes it. A column with only 500 different names shrinks to small numbers plus one list of the names, as Column stores and compression showed.

The Try it writes both designs as Parquet files. Parquet is a common file format for tables stored by column. It cuts a file into row groups, slices of rows, and notes each column's smallest and largest value in every slice. The star's files take 10.8 MB and an 18-column big table takes 14.6 MB. The same question takes 8 ms (thousandths of a second) on the star and 7 ms on the big table. The star's two joins cost almost nothing here. The engine turns each small table into a hash table, a lookup structure that finds a key in one step, and checks every payment against it.

You may be thinking, "Then one big table wins: barely bigger, a little faster, simpler to query." Its price shows up when something changes. Payments are history: once captured, a payment stays what it was. Descriptions of shops change, and some turn out to have been wrong all along. Say shop 7's category was wrong. The star fixes one row of a 500-row table. The big table has to rewrite all 1,958 of shop 7's payments. Its file is stored in date order and shop 7 takes payments every day, so those rows sit in all 9 of its row groups. In practice, that's the whole file.

**One big table is a copy, not the record. Build it from the star when a dashboard needs one.** A copy built that way can be thrown away and rebuilt whenever a dimension changes.

A wrong category is the easy kind of change, because nobody wants the old value back. Next, we'll take a shop that really changed, and ask what last month's report should say about it.

try.title: Store the same payments as a star and as one big table
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `ObtDemo`. It writes the star's three tables, and a big table that already holds the joins, to Parquet files under `labs/bigdata/build/l10/obt`. It compares their sizes and the time of one question, then counts what fixing one shop's category would rewrite.
Predict: how much bigger is a table that repeats 11 dimension columns on every one of a million rows? Twice the size? Ten times?
Why can't the smallest and largest values that Parquet notes per row group narrow the correction down to a few row groups?

code.title: ObtDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l10.demo

import java.io.File

/**
 * The same million payments stored two ways as Parquet: a star (a fact file and two small
 * dimension files) and one big table, with every dimension column copied onto every fact row.
 * Compares the bytes on disk, the time of the same question, and what one correction costs.
 */
fun main() {
    val dir = File(DEMO_DIR, "obt").apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() }
    duck().use { c ->
        rawTables(c, 1_000_000)
        buildStar(c)
        // one big table: the joins done once, at write time
        c.run("""
            CREATE TABLE obt AS
            SELECT f.*, d.day, d.day_name, d.is_weekend, d.month, d.quarter,
                   m.merchant_id, m.merchant_name, m.mcc, m.category, m.risk_tier, m.country
            FROM fact_payment f
            JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
            JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key
            ORDER BY f.date_key, f.payment_id""")
        for (t in listOf("fact_payment", "dim_date", "dim_merchant", "obt")) {
            File(dir, t).mkdirs()
            c.run("COPY $t TO '${File(dir, "$t/data.parquet").absolutePath}' (FORMAT parquet)")
        }
        fun p(t: String) = "read_parquet('${File(dir, "$t/data.parquet").absolutePath}')"
        val star = megabytes(File(dir, "fact_payment")) + megabytes(File(dir, "dim_date")) + megabytes(File(dir, "dim_merchant"))
        println("on disk: star %.1f MB (fact %.1f MB, dimensions %.3f MB), one big table %.1f MB".format(
            star, megabytes(File(dir, "fact_payment")), megabytes(File(dir, "dim_date")) + megabytes(File(dir, "dim_merchant")),
            megabytes(File(dir, "obt"))))
        val columns = c.rows("SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'obt'").first()[0]
        println("one big table: $columns columns; the fact table: 7")

        val starQuery = """
            SELECT m.category, d.is_weekend, count(*), sum(f.amount_cents)
            FROM ${p("fact_payment")} f
            JOIN ${p("dim_date")} d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
            JOIN ${p("dim_merchant")} m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key
            WHERE f.status = 'CAPTURED' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2"""
        val obtQuery = """
            SELECT category, is_weekend, count(*), sum(amount_cents)
            FROM ${p("obt")} WHERE status = 'CAPTURED' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2"""
        val (a, ta) = best(7) { c.rows(starQuery) }
        val (b, tb) = best(7) { c.rows(obtQuery) }
        println("same question from Parquet, best of 7: star with 2 joins %.0f ms, one big table %.0f ms, same answer: %s".format(ta, tb, a == b))

        // a correction: merchant 7's category was wrong all along
        val obtRows = c.rows("SELECT count(*) FROM obt WHERE merchant_id = 7").first()[0]
        val obtGroups = c.rows("SELECT count(DISTINCT row_group_id) FROM parquet_metadata('${File(dir, "obt/data.parquet").absolutePath}')").first()[0]
        // the row groups whose min/max for merchant_id can't rule merchant 7 out: all of them must be rewritten
        val touched = c.rows("""
            SELECT count(*) FROM parquet_metadata('${File(dir, "obt/data.parquet").absolutePath}')
            WHERE path_in_schema = 'merchant_id'
              AND CAST(stats_min_value AS INTEGER) <= 7 AND CAST(stats_max_value AS INTEGER) >= 7""").first()[0]
        println("fix merchant 7's category: star rewrites 1 row of dim_merchant (500 rows);")
        println("  one big table rewrites $obtRows rows of merchant 7, spread over $touched of its $obtGroups row groups")
    }
}

on disk: star 10.8 MB (fact 10.8 MB, dimensions 0.010 MB), one big table 14.6 MB
one big table: 18 columns; the fact table: 7
same question from Parquet, best of 7: star with 2 joins 8 ms, one big table 7 ms, same answer: true
fix merchant 7's category: star rewrites 1 row of dim_merchant (500 rows);

Copying 11 dimension columns onto every payment cost about 35% more disk. That's far less than the raw text would suggest, because each copied column has at most 500 different values and shrinks to small codes. The question was no slower on the star: the two dimensions fit in hash tables of a few kilobytes. The correction is where the designs differ. The star changes one row. The big table has 1,958 rows to change, and the smallest and largest `merchant_id` of the row groups can't rule a single one out, because every day's payments include shop 7. Times vary with your computer; sizes don't.

sections.h: When a shop changes: deciding what the past should say
sections.body:
Payments don't change, but shops do. A shop moves into the high-risk tier, changes category or moves country. Each change raises a question that sounds philosophical and is really about money: should last month's payments count under the shop's old tier, or its new one? Kimball calls a dimension whose rows change now and then a **slowly changing dimension** (SCD), and numbers the possible answers. Two of them do most of the work.

Type 1 overwrites the row. In SQL that's `UPDATE dim_merchant SET risk_tier = 'HIGH' WHERE merchant_id = 1`: change the tier on shop 1's one row. There's still one row per shop and no history, so every report from then on puts old payments under the new tier. That's right for a correction, such as a misspelled name. It's wrong for anything that changed in the world.

In the Try it, 50 shops move to HIGH on 4 November. Rerun the report for 1 to 3 November afterwards, and the high tier's captured money for those days grows from 2.19 billion cents to 4.31 billion, up 97%. Same days, same payments, twice the money in the tier. That's the report from the start of this lesson, and anyone comparing the two runs would want to know what happened.

Type 2 keeps the old row and adds a new one, a new version of the shop. The current version is closed: its `valid_to` becomes the day of the change, and its `is_current` flag becomes false. A new row goes in with the new tier, valid from that day. Each version gets its own **surrogate key** (`merchant_key`), a plain counter that means nothing outside the warehouse. Meanwhile `merchant_id` stays the same on every version and ties them together. A payment's fact row stores the surrogate key of the version that was valid when the payment happened. Payments from before the change point at the LOW version, payments after it at the HIGH version, and no question has to know any dates. The stepper walks through one change.

Two details decide whether type 2 stays right. First, payments arrive late. One made on 3 November may reach the warehouse on 6 November, and it belongs to the old version. So the job that loads the facts must look up the version valid on the payment's day, not the current one. That job is a batch job, a program that works through a pile of input in one run, usually on a schedule. Second, batch jobs get run again after a failure, and applying the same change twice must not create a third version. Orchestrating batch work: DAGs, retries and backfills, lesson 13 of this track, is about exactly that.

Both mistakes fail silently. Every query still runs, and the numbers are quietly wrong. So decide what history means for each column before the first load: overwrite for corrections, a new version for real changes.

Type 2 answers the question "as it was". Sometimes finance wants "as it is": all of a shop's history under today's tier. You get it by going from the payment's version to the shop's `merchant_id`, and from there to its current version. Kimball's types 6 and 7 make that cheaper, and Go deeper lists the rest of his types.

Notice that type 2 changes a row that already exists, when it closes the old version. A warehouse does that for you. Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs, lesson 12, shows what it costs on a table made of files that can't be edited. First, though, let's see how a big warehouse runs a star question at all.

steps: From the `labs` folder, run `ScdDemo`. It builds the star, then moves 50 shops to HIGH on 4 November in two copies of the shop dimension, one type 1 and one type 2. Then it asks both copies for the high tier's captured money on 1 to 3 November.

code.title: ScdDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l10.demo

/**
 * On 2026-11-04 the risk team moves 50 merchants (ids 1, 11, 21, ... 491) to the HIGH tier. The
 * same change is applied to two copies of the star: type 1 (overwrite the dimension row) and
 * type 2 (close the old version, add a new one). Then both answer last week's question: how much
 * captured volume came from HIGH-risk merchants on 1 to 3 November, before the change?
 */
fun main() {
    duck().use { c ->
        rawTables(c, 1_000_000)
        buildStar(c)
        c.run("CREATE TABLE moved AS SELECT CAST(10 * k + 1 AS INTEGER) AS merchant_id FROM range(50) t(k)")
        println("before the change: " + c.rows("SELECT risk_tier, count(*) FROM dim_merchant WHERE merchant_id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM moved) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1")
            .joinToString { "${it[1]} ${it[0]}" } + " merchants are moving to HIGH")

        // type 1: overwrite. One row per merchant, no history
        c.run("CREATE TABLE dim_merchant_t1 AS SELECT * FROM dim_merchant")
        c.run("UPDATE dim_merchant_t1 SET risk_tier = 'HIGH' WHERE merchant_id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM moved)")

        // type 2: close the current version and add a new one with a new surrogate key
        c.run("CREATE TABLE dim_merchant_t2 AS SELECT * FROM dim_merchant")
        c.run("""
            INSERT INTO dim_merchant_t2
            SELECT CAST(500 + row_number() OVER (ORDER BY merchant_id) AS INTEGER), merchant_id, merchant_name, mcc, category,
                   'HIGH', country, DATE '2026-11-04', DATE '9999-12-31', true
            FROM dim_merchant WHERE merchant_id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM moved)""")
        c.run("""
            UPDATE dim_merchant_t2 SET valid_to = DATE '2026-11-04', is_current = false
            WHERE merchant_id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM moved) AND merchant_key <= 500""")
        // payments from 4 November on belong to the new versions
        c.run("CREATE TABLE fact_t2 AS SELECT * FROM fact_payment")
        c.run("""
            UPDATE fact_t2 SET merchant_key = v.merchant_key
            FROM dim_merchant_t2 old, dim_merchant_t2 v
            WHERE fact_t2.merchant_key = old.merchant_key AND v.merchant_id = old.merchant_id AND v.is_current
              AND old.merchant_id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM moved) AND fact_t2.date_key >= 20261104""")

        println("merchant 1 in the type 2 dimension:")
        c.rows("SELECT merchant_key, risk_tier, valid_from, valid_to, is_current FROM dim_merchant_t2 WHERE merchant_id = 1 ORDER BY valid_from")
            .forEach { println("  merchant_key=%-4s risk_tier=%-6s valid %s to %s, is_current=%s".format(it[0], it[1], it[2], it[3], it[4])) }

        fun highBeforeChange(fact: String, dim: String) = c.rows("""
            SELECT sum(f.amount_cents) FROM $fact f JOIN $dim m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key
            WHERE f.status = 'CAPTURED' AND m.risk_tier = 'HIGH' AND f.date_key < 20261104""").first()[0] as Number
        val t1 = highBeforeChange("fact_payment", "dim_merchant_t1").toLong()
        val t2 = highBeforeChange("fact_t2", "dim_merchant_t2").toLong()
        val then = highBeforeChange("fact_payment", "dim_merchant").toLong()
        println("HIGH-risk captured volume on 1 to 3 November:")
        println("  what the report said on 3 November:  %,16d cents".format(then))
        println("  type 1, asked again after the change: %,16d cents (+%.0f%%)".format(t1, 100.0 * (t1 - then) / then))
        println("  type 2, asked again after the change: %,16d cents".format(t2))
    }
}

aside.title: Why does a shop need a second number when it already has an id?
aside.body: Under type 2, one shop has several rows, one per version, and each payment must point at exactly one of them. The shop's id, 1, is the same on every version, so it can't tell them apart. The surrogate key can: key 2 is shop 1 while it was LOW, and key 501 is shop 1 since it became HIGH. Making it a plain counter that means nothing outside the warehouse is on purpose. If the payments program ever reuses or renumbers its ids, the warehouse's keys don't move.

sections.h: How big warehouses run a star question without moving the payments
sections.body:
A star question always has the same shape: one huge table, a few small ones, filters on the small ones and sums over the huge one. Engines built for analytics are designed around that shape. Column stores and compression covered how they store it: each column apart, squeezed, with a zone map per chunk. A zone map is a note of the chunk's smallest and largest value, so a chunk that can't match is skipped unread. This section is about how they join it.

A big warehouse spreads its fact table over many machines, each holding a share of the rows. The shuffle, partitioning and joins (lesson 7 of this track) met two ways to join tables spread like that. A sort-merge join sends rows across the network to the machine in charge of their key, a step called a shuffle. Here that would move a billion payments to meet 500 shop rows. A broadcast hash join sends the small table to every machine instead. Each machine builds a hash table from it and streams its own payments past it, where they already sit. For a star, that's almost always the right plan: every machine gets every dimension, and the fact table never moves. A 2016 paper by the people who built Snowflake describes star questions in exactly those terms.

That's where the bookkeeper's card files stop being a good picture. A bookkeeper fetches one card at a time. A warehouse copies the whole card file to every machine, filters it first, and then uses what's left to skip whole pages of the journal unread.

Here's how the skipping works. Say the question asks for weekends and high-risk shops. Once the engine has built hash tables from the filtered dimensions, it knows every `date_key` and `merchant_key` that can possibly match: two dates and 50 shops. It turns them into a filter on its read of the fact table, while the question runs. The zone maps then skip every chunk whose dates hold no weekend.

In the Try it, over 4 million payments stored in date order, DuckDB's plan shows that filter as `date_key IN (20261101, 20261107)` plus a list of shop keys. The read covers 11 of 33 row groups and passes 47,775 rows to the join. With that step switched off, it reads all 33 and passes 1,599,756 rows, for the join to throw away. Spark does the same, and calls it dynamic partition pruning.

The three big cloud warehouses run star questions this way, each with its own controls. Snowflake keeps tables as files that are never changed, on S3, Amazon's cloud file store. It runs questions on groups of rented machines that it starts and stops as needed. A separate service keeps the list of each table's files with their statistics, and skips files before a question starts and again during the join. BigQuery is Google's warehouse. It runs a question as a tree of workers over columnar storage and keeps the shuffle in memory, and Google's own guide says a star already suits it well.

Redshift is Amazon's warehouse, a group of machines in which each one holds a slice of every table, and you choose how rows are spread. KEY distribution puts rows with the same key on the same slice, so a fact table and a large dimension spread on their join key meet without moving. ALL keeps a full copy of a table on every machine: a broadcast decided when the data is loaded. The default, AUTO, starts small tables as ALL and changes them as they grow. Amazon's guide adds that forcing ALL rarely pays, because copying a small table during a question is cheap.

What you control is the same everywhere. Keep dimensions small, and store facts sorted by the column most questions filter on, usually the date. The engine does the rest.

All of this rests on one thing the warehouse does for you: it keeps the list of each table's files, inside its own product, and changes that list all at once. Without that list, a table is only a folder of files.

SELECT m.category, d.is_weekend,
       count(*), sum(f.amount_cents)
FROM fact_payment f
JOIN dim_date d     ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key
WHERE f.status = 'CAPTURED'
GROUP BY m.category, d.is_weekend;

compare.note: Both return the same eight rows, and in a column store both read only the columns they name. The one on the right is shorter to write and skips the joins. That matters little when the dimensions fit in a few kilobytes of hash table, as in the demo (8 ms against 7 ms). The real difference is upkeep: the star corrects a shop in one dimension row, while the big table rewrites every payment of that shop. Keep the star as the record, and build a big table from it when a dashboard needs one.

worked.title: Design a star for the nightly payout report

steps.say: Each night the company pays every shop what its card payments brought in, minus refunds and the company's fee. That's a payout, and one payout covers many payments. Declare the grain first, in one sentence, because every other choice follows from it. The report adds up what each shop is paid, so one row is one payout line: one captured payment inside one payout.
steps.code:
grain: one row per payout line
       (one captured payment in one payout to one shop)

steps.say: List what analysts filter and group by (the dimensions) and what they add up (the measures). Ids that name a line but describe nothing, such as the payout's number, stay on the fact row as degenerate dimensions.
steps.code:
dimensions: date (payout day), merchant (type 2: tier and category change),
            card country, currency
measures:   gross_cents, fee_cents, net_cents
degenerate: payout_batch_id, payment_id

steps.say: Write the fact table: surrogate keys into the dimensions, the degenerate ids and the measures. Nothing descriptive goes here.
steps.code:
CREATE TABLE fact_payout_line (
    date_key         INTEGER NOT NULL,   -- yyyymmdd of the payout day
    merchant_key     INTEGER NOT NULL,   -- the shop version valid that day
    card_country_key SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    currency_key     SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    payout_batch_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,    -- degenerate dimension
    payment_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
    gross_cents      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    fee_cents        BIGINT NOT NULL,
    net_cents        BIGINT NOT NULL
);

steps.say: Check that each measure can be added up. `net_cents` adds up across every dimension: per month, per tier, per shop. The money the company holds for a shop at the end of each day would not. You can add those balances across shops on one day, but adding Monday's balance to Tuesday's counts the same money twice. Kimball calls such a measure semi-additive, and it belongs in a separate fact table with one row per shop per day.
steps.code:
SELECT d.month, m.risk_tier, sum(f.net_cents)        -- additive: fine across days
FROM fact_payout_line f
JOIN dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_key = f.merchant_key
GROUP BY d.month, m.risk_tier;

-- a balance is semi-additive: add it up per day, never over days

steps: From the `labs` folder, run the tests with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code, and all nine fail for now on `TODO`s. Each test class opens an in-memory DuckDB database, loads the raw tables from `RawData` (the week from Sunday 2026-11-01, 500 shops) and creates the empty star with the given `createTables` and `loadDates`. Read `RawData.kt` and `createTables` first: they define every table and column.

hints: Keys in order: `CAST(row_number() OVER (ORDER BY m.merchant_id) AS INTEGER)`. The date key of a timestamp: `CAST(strftime(p.created_at, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER)`.

The version valid on a day: `m.valid_from <= CAST(p.created_at AS DATE) AND CAST(p.created_at AS DATE) < m.valid_to`. To skip rows already loaded: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fact_payment f WHERE f.payment_id = p.payment_id)`. `executeUpdate` returns the number of rows it added.

In `applyScd2`, set `c.autoCommit = false`, so your statements run as one transaction. For each change, read the current version (`WHERE merchant_id = ? AND is_current`), and skip the change if the tier and the category code are equal. Otherwise `UPDATE ... SET valid_to = ?, is_current = false WHERE merchant_key = ?`, then `INSERT ... SELECT (SELECT max(merchant_key) FROM dim_merchant) + 1, ...` copying the other columns from the old version. `RawData.category(mcc)` gives the new category name. Commit at the end, and roll back (undo everything) on an exception.
As is: join the payment's version `v`, then `dim_merchant cur ON cur.merchant_id = v.merchant_id AND cur.is_current`, and group by `cur.risk_tier`.

drill.title: A type 2 change in two statements
drill.prompt: From memory, write the SQL that moves shop 42 to the HIGH tier from 2026-11-04 as a type 2 change in `dim_merchant(merchant_key, merchant_id, merchant_name, mcc, category, risk_tier, country, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)`. Then write the join that gives each payment the shop version valid on its day, when loading from `raw_payments(payment_id, merchant_id, created_at, ...)`.

answer.src:
-- 1. close the current version (inside one transaction with step 2)
UPDATE dim_merchant
SET valid_to = DATE '2026-11-04', is_current = false
WHERE merchant_id = 42 AND is_current;

-- 2. add the new version with the next surrogate key
INSERT INTO dim_merchant
SELECT (SELECT max(merchant_key) FROM dim_merchant) + 1, merchant_id, merchant_name, mcc, category,
       'HIGH', country, DATE '2026-11-04', DATE '9999-12-31', true
FROM dim_merchant
WHERE merchant_id = 42 AND valid_to = DATE '2026-11-04';

-- 3. a fact row gets the version valid on its day, not the current one
SELECT p.payment_id, m.merchant_key
FROM raw_payments p
JOIN dim_merchant m
  ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id
 AND m.valid_from <= CAST(p.created_at AS DATE)
 AND CAST(p.created_at AS DATE) < m.valid_to;

recap: A warehouse keeps analytics data as a star: a fact table of events at a declared grain (keys plus numbers to add up), with dimension tables around it that describe who, what, where and when.

A star keeps each dimension flat, one join away. A snowflake splits dimensions into more tables and more joins. One big table copies every description onto every fact: column compression makes it cheap to store, and corrections make it costly to keep.

When a shop changes, type 1 overwrites its row and rewrites history. Type 2 closes the current version and adds a new one with a new surrogate key, and each payment keeps the key of the version valid on its day.
Load facts by the version valid on the payment's day, so late payments land right, and make every load safe to run twice.
Warehouses copy small dimensions to every machine, turn the keys that survive the dimension filters into a filter on the fact table's read, and skip chunks by their zone maps.
The limit: all of this assumes a warehouse that keeps each table's list of files for you and changes rows when asked. On plain files in cheap storage, nobody does that yet.
closing:
We started with a report that said 21.9 million one day and 43.1 million a week later, for the same three days. One row per shop had rewritten the past. A second version of each changed shop keeps it.

When a banking app shows your spending by category, ask what would happen if the bank moved one shop from Restaurants to Groceries. Should last year's chart change? Either can be right, but someone has to choose.

Next, we'll build a table's list of files ourselves with Apache Iceberg, a free set of rules and code for keeping tables in files. The question: how can a table made of many files change in one step, so nobody reads half a write?

quiz.q: Someone asks for a fact table of "payments and their refunds". Some payments get two partial refunds. What do you settle first?
options: The grain: for example one row per payment event (a capture or a refund), so a payment with two refunds is several rows
The dimensions, then columns `refund_1_cents` and `refund_2_cents` on the payment's row
A rule that `payment_id` must be unique, so each payment is exactly one row
Nothing yet: load whatever arrives and decide later
quiz.why: Every other decision depends on what one row means. With one row per payment event, two refunds are two rows, and every amount adds up. A column per refund breaks on the third refund and makes sums awkward. One row per payment forces you to squeeze events into columns. Loading first and deciding later gives a table whose rows mean different things.

quiz.q: A shop's name was saved as "Merhcant 42" because of a typo when it signed up. How should the dimension take the fix?
options: Type 2: close the version and add one with the right spelling
Type 3: keep the misspelled name in a `previous_name` column
Type 1: overwrite the name on the shop's rows
Type 0: names never change
quiz.why: A typo is a correction, not a change in the world. No report should ever group payments under the misspelled name, so rewriting history is exactly what you want. Type 2 is the tempting answer, because it feels safer to keep everything. But it would keep the wrong spelling as a real-looking past version, and split the shop's history in two for no reason.

quiz.q: A payment made on 3 November reaches the warehouse on 6 November. Shop 7 moved to HIGH on 4 November, kept as type 2. The fact load matches every payment to the shop's current version. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the current version is the one the shop has
The load fails, because the payment's date is before the version's `valid_from`
The payment is loaded twice, once per version
The payment points at the HIGH version, so as-was reports count a 3 November payment under HIGH
quiz.why: Type 2 only works if each payment gets the version valid on its own day. Matching to the current version quietly files late payments under the new tier, which is exactly the history type 2 was meant to keep. Nothing fails, and that's why the mistake survives for months. The fix is the validity-range join from the lab.

quiz.q: Which change hurts a one-big-table design the most?
options: Adding another day of payments
Correcting the category of a shop that has two years of payments
Adding a dashboard that groups by weekday
Moving the table to a faster disk
quiz.why: In a big table, the category is copied onto every one of the shop's payments, so a correction rewrites them all, and they're spread through every file of two years of data. In a star, it's one dimension row. Adding a day is the easy case for both designs, and grouping by a column the table already has needs no change at all.

quiz.q: From The shuffle, partitioning and joins: a star question on a Spark cluster of 50 machines joins a fact table of 3 billion payments to a 500-row shop dimension on `merchant_key`. Which plan do you want to see?
options: A sort-merge join: both tables shuffled across the network by `merchant_key`
A broadcast hash join: the 500 rows copied to every machine, and the payments never moved
A shuffled hash join: both tables sent across the network by key, then joined with a hash table
A cartesian product, every payment paired with every shop, then filtered by `merchant_key`
quiz.why: With one side tiny, broadcasting it costs 500 rows times 50 machines. A sort-merge join would move 3 billion payments across the network to meet them, and so would a shuffled hash join. Every warehouse prefers the broadcast for star joins, and it's why Redshift's ALL distribution exists: a broadcast decided when the data is loaded.

flashcards.front: What is the grain of a fact table?
flashcards.back: What one row means, decided before anything else: one row per payment, per payout line, or per shop per day.

flashcards.front: Fact table or dimension table: which one is long and narrow?
flashcards.back: The fact table: one row per event, with keys and numbers to add up. Dimensions are short and wide: descriptions of who, what, where and when.

flashcards.front: What does a type 2 slowly changing dimension do when a shop changes?
flashcards.back: It closes the current version (`valid_to` = the day of the change, `is_current` = false) and adds a new version with a new surrogate key, valid from that day.

flashcards.front: Why does a type 2 dimension need surrogate keys?
flashcards.back: Several versions share one shop id, so each version needs its own key. A payment stores the key of the version valid when it happened.
A star keeps each dimension in one flat table (one join). A snowflake splits dimensions into smaller tables (more joins). Analysts mostly prefer the star.

flashcards.front: What is a run-time join filter in a star question?
flashcards.back: The engine collects the keys that survive the dimension filters and turns them into a filter on the fact table's read, so zone maps can skip chunks: 11 of 33 row groups were read in the demo.

flashcards.front: Redshift's KEY and ALL distribution: what does each do?
flashcards.back: KEY puts rows with the same key on the same machine, so tables spread on their join key meet without moving. ALL copies the whole table to every machine: a broadcast decided when the data is loaded.

terms.plain: Online analytical processing: questions that read many rows to add them up, asked a few times a day. Its opposite, OLTP, touches a few rows by key, thousands of times a second.
A separate database built for analytical questions, loaded with copies of the data the business runs on.
The table of events, one row per event at a declared grain, holding numbers to add up and keys into the dimensions.
A table that describes who, what, where or when, with the columns questions filter and group by.
What one row of a fact table stands for, such as one payment.
A fact table with flat dimension tables around it, each one join away.
A dimension whose rows change now and then, with a chosen rule for history: overwrite (type 1), add a version (type 2) and others.
A number the warehouse gives each version of a dimension row. The business id, such as the shop id, stays the same across versions.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to someone in finance why the warehouse keeps two rows for shop 7, and how a report about last week still puts its payments under the tier they had then.
explain_back.answer: Shop 7 changed tier on 4 November, from LOW to HIGH. If we had overwritten its one row, every report would now show all of its past payments as high-risk, including reports about days before the change, and rerunning last week's report would give a different number. So the warehouse keeps versions instead. The old row is closed: it says LOW, valid from 1 November until 4 November. A new row says HIGH, valid from 4 November with no end yet. Each version has its own number inside the warehouse. When a payment is loaded, it gets the number of the version that was valid on the day it was made, even if the payment arrives a few days late. A report that matches payments to shops on that number sees each payment with the tier it had at the time, so last week's payments stay under LOW. If you want the other view, all of the shop's history under today's tier, we can go through the shop's id to its current version instead. Both answers are right; they answer different questions, and each report should say which one it uses.

deeper.body:
**The rest of Kimball's change types.** Type 0 never changes a column at all, such as the day a shop signed up. Type 3 keeps one previous value in an extra column (`previous_tier`), which is enough for exactly one change. Type 4 moves columns that change often into a small dimension of their own, so the main one doesn't grow a version per change. Types 6 and 7 serve "as it is" reports cheaply: type 6 keeps a current-value column on every version, and type 7 puts a second key on each payment that always leads to the current version.

**More kinds of fact table.** Ours is a transaction fact table, one row per event. A periodic snapshot has one row per shop per day with a balance. An accumulating snapshot has one row per payment that is updated as the payment moves through its steps, from the tap to the payout. Measures are additive, semi-additive (balances: add them across shops, never across days) or non-additive (ratios: work them out again from their parts). **Conformed dimensions** are dimensions shared by several fact tables, such as one `dim_merchant` used for payments, refunds and payouts, so their reports line up.

**Tools that keep type 2 rules for you.** PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, added temporal keys in version 18. A primary key declared as `PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, valid_during WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` on a column holding a date range refuses two versions of a shop whose validity overlaps, which is the rule the lab's last test checks by hand. Spark 4.3's Declarative Pipelines can maintain a type 2 table from a feed of changes (`CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC INTO`), written into a table format that supports row-level changes, such as Apache Iceberg from the next lesson. And dbt, a tool that runs a project's SQL transformations inside a warehouse, has snapshots for the same job.

**Reading on.** Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition) covers star and snowflake schemas and one big table in chapter 3, and column storage and query execution for this kind of work in chapter 4. For the products, read the Snowflake paper's sections on skipping files, Amazon's guide to Redshift's distribution and sort keys, and Google's Dremel paper, which describes the system behind BigQuery.
